story.text: What do we *gain* by applying Friedrich Pohlmann’s term “systematically manufactured lack of structure” (systematisch hergestellte Strukturlosigkeit) to the US presidency since 2024, if we do so not as a strict historical comparison to National Socialism but as a reuse of a diagnostic concept from Arendtian totalitarianism studies?

Using “systematically manufactured lack of structure” as a diagnostic term for the US presidency since 2024 helps us notice and name a governing style that intentionally erodes stable structures of responsibility, information and procedure, thereby normalising chaos as a mode of rule; the gain is analytical clarity about how power can be exercised through the creation of confusion, without claiming equivalence of regime type or historical scale.

Because the phrase comes from analyses of National Socialism, reusing it forces us to look specifically at *how* structures are weakened: not by mere incompetence, but by repeated moves that blur chains of command, hollow out institutions, and replace predictable processes with ad hoc decisions, making it harder for others to locate responsibility or mount organised resistance.

When we describe the current US presidency as operating through systematically manufactured lack of structure, we shift the focus from the leader’s personality or “style” to the patterned effects on institutions, norms, and informational environments, which is exactly the move Arendt wanted when she distinguished structural features of total domination from moralising talk about “bad leaders”.

The term highlights that chaos can be a *resource* of power, not just a by-product: if nobody knows which rule will be applied tomorrow, which statement is binding, or which staffer will survive the week, then everyone must constantly re-orient around the leader’s latest signal, producing dependency and self-censorship even in the absence of formal repression.

For observers and critics, the concept offers a shared handle (“Strukturlosigkeit”) that condenses many scattered impressions—staff churn, policy whiplash, contradictory messaging, procedural short-circuits—into a single pattern, making it easier to connect dots across episodes and talk about them in a more than anecdotal way.

Using a concept with an Arendtian provenance also keeps our attention on the relation between structure, judgment and worldliness: when structures that stabilise a shared world are systematically undermined, it becomes harder for citizens to form and exchange sound political judgments—this links contemporary US developments back into our larger Arendt project.

Reusing a term coined in the context of National Socialism risks semantic inflation: even if we carefully say “this is not a historical comparison”, the provenance of the phrase can still invite listeners to hear an implied equivalence between the US presidency and a totalitarian regime, which may shut down rather than open up public conversation.

Framing the US presidency since 2024 under a single strong label like “systematically manufactured lack of structure” can obscure countervailing tendencies in the same system—robust judicial pushback, electoral alternation, surviving bureaucratic routines—and thereby overstate the coherence and success of the “program” we are trying to describe.

The concept may tempt us to read all disorganisation as intentional strategy; this can flatten important distinctions between deliberate structural sabotage, ordinary partisanship, and plain incompetence, and may reduce our own analytical sharpness by treating “lack of structure” as a catch-all explanation.

Because the US political system remains formally constitutional and pluralistic, focusing too much on “manufactured Strukturlosigkeit” at the presidential level might underplay how much structural power is still exercised through very conventional means (legislation, appointments, budget politics), and thus mislead activists about where effective counter-measures lie.
